findings.reason: the scan needs a stated rule for a `children` entry that is not attributable to the owner (or an explicit, recorded acceptance that a pre-fix record may re-adopt), otherwise the node implements a recovery path that revives the incident it was written to close. The previous-record source is safe for sessions the owner itself dispatched and unsafe for sessions another session dispatched and this owner's earlier host wrongly kept.
findings.text: the start-up scan admits any session named in the previous `children` list, but that list is exactly what a host records for every pair it ran, including the foreign pair §1 records (nova-39's host holding nova-8a's session `35a66cc6`); §3's guard sits in `_request_host_follower` and is not on this path, because the host calls `handle()` directly rather than composing a request, so a re-armed host can re-adopt the foreign session and take its single-follower lock — the outcome §1 exists to stop — from a record written before the fix.

findings.reason: the sentence is one clause the worker either codes or skips with no effect on the test — the fourth case fails without the field and passes with it, and a second force write at start is harmless because `_write_record` compares everything but `updated_at`.
findings.text: "It records in its `session-hosts` record that it is waiting for a dispatch, then serves its FIFO as today" is stated as a new write, but `supervise` already calls `self._write_record(force=True)` as its first act (`reckon/crew/session_host.py:667`), so the only change is the new field; read as written a worker may add a second start-up write or treat the requirement as already met.
